paragraphs.text: Some tell us that this and the two following psalms were the great Hallelujah sung at solemn times in their assemblies. But others say better, that the great Hallelujah (as the Hebrews called it) began at Psa 113:1-9., and held on till Psa 119:1-176, which they at the passover began to sing after that cup of wine they called Poculum hymni seu laudationis.

paragraphs.text: Gen 12:17; Gen 20:3. Kings and queens must not think themselves too good to nurse God’s little ones, yea, to do them homage, licking up the dust under their feet, Isa 49:23.

paragraphs.text: This God speaketh not of kings, but to kings, concerning his people who have an unction from the Father, being sanctified and set apart for his peculiar. To touch these is to touch the apple of God’s eye, Zec 2:8; they are sacred persons.
paragraphs.anchor: Touch not mine anointed, &c.

paragraphs.text: The patriarchs were such, Gen 20:7, so are still all godly ministers, whom they who harm by word or deed have not so much knowledge as Pilate’s wife had in a dream. See Psa 14:4.
paragraphs.anchor: And do my prophets no harm

paragraphs.text: How easy is it with God soon to starve us all by denying us a harvest or two! If he do but call for a famine it is done.

paragraphs.text: Either by withdrawing bread, that staff of man’s life, or his blessing from it; for man liveth not by bread alone (or at all), but by every word, &c., Mat 4:4, without which bread can no more nourish us than a clod of clay, In pane conclusus est quasi baculus, qui nos sustineat. See Hag 1:6. {See Trapp on "Hag 1:6"}

Jacob’s best and happiest days were those he spent in Egypt.

paragraphs.text: Seeking to imbase and enervate their spirits by base drudgeries imposed upon them. So afterwards dealt the Persian tyrant with Hormisaus, and the Great Turk with the Christians.

paragraphs.text: Heb. the words of his signs; for God’s wondrous works are vocal, they are real sermons of God’s power and justice. See Exo 4:8.

paragraphs.text: Palpable darkness, by reason of most black and thick vapours of the earth mingling themselves with the air; such as Aben Ezra said that he once felt, sailing upon the ocean, the gross vapours there putting out the light of fire and candle, and not suffering them to be re-enkindled.
paragraphs.anchor: He sent darkness

paragraphs.text: They, that is, the plagues called for, came immediately, with an Ecce me. Or, they, that is, Moses and Aaron, refused not to denounce and inflict those plagues, though Pharaoh threatened to kill them; where a man would wonder at Pharaoh’s hardness and hardiness, that being in the midst of that deep and dreadful darkness, he could rage against God, and threaten with death his servant Moses. The Arabic (reading ìå for ìà) rendereth it, Et irritarunt sermonem eius; and they (the Egyptians) provoked his word, or rebelled against it.
paragraphs.anchor: And they rebelled not against his word

paragraphs.text: A just hand of God upon them for their cruelty in drowning the Hebrew infants, and a real forewarning, if they could have seen it, of the death of their firstborn, and their final overthrow at the Red Sea.
paragraphs.anchor: And he turned their waters into blood

paragraphs.text: Which was a great part of their food; piscis a pascendo dictus.

paragraphs.text: Like grass that grows upon the ground, or as fishes spawned in the sea, as the word signifieth, Gen 1:20. Some think they were not common frogs, sed venenatas et horrendas, quales sunt rubetae et bufones, but toads and lizards; crocodiles, some think, came out of the river, and destroyed people (Aben-Ezra).
paragraphs.anchor: The land brought forth frogs in abundance

paragraphs.text: Regis et regulorum inter medias enses, medias custodias; this was the finger of God; as it was likewise when a town in Spain was overturned by conies, and another in Thessaly by moles, a city in France undone by frogs, and another in Africa by locusts (Plin. l. viii. c. 29).

paragraphs.anchor: And lice in all their coasts
